angle: No seat limits, purely usage-based, and a 20-person team: why a full sales process on every signup is impossible
post_first_line: A team of 20-something can't sell to everyone.
linkedin_post:
A team of 20-something can't sell to everyone.

Dima Khlopkov's team hit a wall that most growth-stage companies run into eventually.

The volume of signups and leads coming in was huge for the size of the team. Running a full sales process on every one of them was simply impossible.

So the pricing model changed. There are no limits now. It's purely usage-based.

Dima described the current setup as a hybrid approach. The change happened about 4 months ago, maybe 5.

The constraint wasn't demand. It was headcount. The model had to fit the team, not the other way around.

If every lead needs a human to move forward, a lean team becomes the bottleneck.

Where does your sales process break first as volume grows?

Slide 2: Signups and leads kept coming in at serious volume.
Slide 3: A full sales process on every lead was impossible.
Slide 4: So the model changed: no limits, purely usage-based.
Slide 5: Today it's a hybrid approach, shifted about 4 months ago.
Slide 6: The constraint wasn't demand. It was headcount.
Slide 7: Design the model around the team you actually have.

lesson.title: When your team can't touch every lead
takeaways: A lean team facing high signup volume cannot run a full sales process on everyone.
Usage-based pricing with no limits lets people get value without a sales conversation.
A hybrid approach keeps human effort where it matters while the model handles the rest.
lesson.exercise: Count your monthly signups and divide by the number of people who can run a full sales process. If the number is unrealistic, list which leads truly need a human and which could move forward on their own.

angle: From easy to hard PLG signals: from 30-day inactivity to a power user who changes jobs and champions you at the new company
post_first_line: Dima Khlopkov's easiest PLG signal: a 30-day inactive user.
linkedin_post:
Dima Khlopkov's easiest PLG signal: a 30-day inactive user.

Dima's hardest one takes real work to catch.

The simple end: someone goes quiet for about 30 days, then logs in again. That's a signal, and it takes almost nothing to set up.

The hard end: a power user switches jobs, lands in a new workspace, and starts trying out Gumloop, even on a free package. Dima wants to know the moment that happens.

That person can approach the new company already excited. They can champion the product in the new org.

Signals run on a spectrum, from very simple to advanced and hard to get.

But Dima's advice is not to overthink it. Implement whatever comes to mind first, then iterate across different places and sequences.

Start with the obvious signal. Get the hard ones later.

lesson.title: Start with simple PLG signals, then build toward hard ones
takeaways: Signals range from simple, like a user returning after about 30 days inactive, to advanced, like a power user showing up at a new company.
A power user trying the product in a new workspace can become a champion in the new org.
Overthinking signals is a mistake. Implement the first ideas that come to mind and iterate.
lesson.exercise: List every PLG signal you can think of in 10 minutes, rank them from easiest to hardest, and set up the easiest one this week.

angle: A 3-tier outbound system: manual for top accounts, semi-automated in the middle, fully automated for the rest
post_first_line: Three tiers. Three levels of automation.
linkedin_post:
Three tiers. Three levels of automation.

Dima Khlopkov shared how the Unify team splits outbound so effort goes where it matters most.

Tier 1 is the most manual. The GTM team writes manual emails and refines them by hand. There may be a link between the head of sales or a founder and that individual, a detail worth mentioning that an AI agent with a web search could never find.

Tier 2 is semi-automated. The emails are automated, but the LinkedIn steps stay manual. The goal is to diversify how those accounts get touched.

Tier 3 gets a fully automated sequence.

The point is that not every account deserves the same amount of human effort. Personal connections are worth the manual work. Everything else shouldn't eat your team's time.

How do you split effort across your accounts?

Slide 2: Tier 1 is manual: hand-refined emails from your team.
Slide 3: Use connections between your founders and the prospect.
Slide 4: Some details are impossible for an AI agent to find.
Slide 5: Tier 2 is semi-automated: automated emails, manual LinkedIn steps.
Slide 6: Mixing automated and manual steps diversifies your touches.
Slide 7: Tier 3 runs a fully automated sequence.
Slide 8: Match the human effort to the account.

lesson.title: Build a 3-tier outbound system
takeaways: Tier 1 accounts get manual steps and hand-refined emails, especially when a founder or sales leader has a personal link.
Tier 2 accounts get automated emails with manual LinkedIn steps to diversify touches.
Tier 3 accounts get a fully automated sequence.
lesson.exercise: Sort your target accounts into three groups. For your top group, find one non-obvious personal connection to mention in a manual email.

angle: Timing beats messaging: reach people the week they try your product, and name-drop a teammate
linkedin_post:
Timing beats messaging. Every time.

Dima Khlopkov shared the one variable our team trusts most when reaching out to new users.

The moment someone tries a product like Gumloop, they're excited about the platform. Dima points out that's probably the best state to start a conversation with them.

So the message itself stays simple. It's personalized by role: GTM teams are using Gumloop for this and that, marketing teams are using it for something else.

Then comes the part Dima thinks changes the game: name-dropping people.

In Dima's view, name-dropping is a different level of personalization, because you can't really source that information from the internet.

The takeaway: stop polishing copy for weeks. Get the timing right, keep the message short, and add one detail nobody can scrape.

Where do you spend more effort: timing or copy?
carousel: Slide 1: Timing beats messaging at every level.
Slide 2: Someone who just tried your product is excited right now.
Slide 3: That excitement is the best moment to start a conversation.
Slide 4: Keep the message simple and personalize by role.
Slide 5: GTM teams use us for this, marketing teams for that.
Slide 6: Then name-drop people to take personalization up a level.
Slide 7: You can't source that detail from the internet.
Slide 8: Perfect the timing first, then polish the copy.

lesson.title: Timing First, Then a Name Drop
takeaways: Reach people while they're excited about a recent product trial, since that's when they're most open to a conversation.
Keep the message simple and personalize it by role instead of rewriting copy for every person.
Name-dropping people adds personalization that can't be sourced from the internet.
lesson.exercise: Pick one trigger, like a recent product trial. Write a two-line role-based message and add one real teammate name, then send it within the same week.

angle: 10-12% reply rates from acting on one LinkedIn signal: who viewed your founder's profile
post_first_line: 10 to 12% reply rates. From one signal.
linkedin_post:
10 to 12% reply rates. From one signal.

Dima Khlopkov's team at Gumloop found the exact moment outreach lands best, and it has nothing to do with a better template.

The signal is LinkedIn activity. A prospect views the founder's profile, views the company page, or engages with the content the team posts. At that point, Gumloop is top of mind for them.

That's the right time to reach out.

Dima's team combines two approaches: inbound-led outbound flows and LinkedIn-based signals. Outreach doesn't feel pushy because it shows up when the prospect is already paying attention.

The result is that they keep reply rates at 10 to 12%.

Most teams pick a side: wait for inbound or blast outbound. The better move is to let inbound attention decide when outbound fires.

Which buyer signal do you act on first?

lesson.title: Let inbound attention trigger your outbound
takeaways: Profile views and content engagement show a prospect has your brand top of mind.
Reaching out right after those signals feels timely instead of pushy.
Combining LinkedIn signals with inbound-led outbound flows kept reply rates at 10 to 12%.
lesson.exercise: List the LinkedIn actions that show interest in your company, such as founder profile views, company page views, and post engagement. Pick one and set up a outreach flow that triggers within a day of it happening.

angle: What's a good positive reply rate? Product signals can run 4x the norm
post_first_line: Product signals can beat reply benchmarks 4x.
linkedin_post:
Product signals can beat reply benchmarks 4x.

But the benchmark most teams chase hides what actually drives that number.

Quintin Smith took a question on what a good positive reply rate looks like. The honest answer is "it depends." Reply rate is largely determined by the type of signal behind the outreach, and it keeps climbing as signals get combined and layered.

Here is the range Quintin shared from the data:

- Positive replies: roughly 0.2 to 1%
- Standard replies overall: 1 to 3%
- Product signals: can be 4x higher than a typical positive reply rate

The reason is simple. Product signal accounts are the warmest accounts you have.

So a single reply rate number matters less than knowing which signal each message was built on. Compare a product signal campaign against a cold list and the gap will look like a broken benchmark, when it is really a difference in intent.

What signal drives your best reply rate today?

Slide 2: Signal type largely determines your reply rate.
Slide 3: Layering and combining signals pushes it even higher.
Slide 4: Positive replies often land around 0.2 to 1%.
Slide 5: Standard replies more commonly sit at 1 to 3%.
Slide 6: Product signals can run 4x a typical positive reply rate.
Slide 7: Those are your warmest accounts, so they respond.
Slide 8: Benchmark each campaign by signal, not one blended number.

lesson.title: Benchmark reply rates by signal type, not as one number
takeaways: Positive reply rate depends heavily on the type of signal behind the outreach.
Layering and combining signals tends to push reply rates higher.
Product signals can produce reply rates around 4x a typical positive reply rate because they surface your warmest accounts.
lesson.exercise: Pull your last 90 days of outreach and group it by signal type. Calculate the positive reply rate for each group, then compare product signal campaigns to everything else.
